title: How Should a Person Die? | The Point Magazine
gist: A personal essay by Zach Marcus on forming a parasocial attachment to former senator Ben Sasse, who is deliberately dying of terminal pancreatic cancer in public via podcasts. Marcus contrasts Sasse's chosen public death as a model of how to die against the involuntary genre of 'dying online' (ISIS videos, Charlie Kirk's killing, 'lolcows'), and traces his own shift from atheist determinism toward belief in souls and a striking absence of death anxiety among religious and classical thinkers.

insights.claim: Ben Sasse announced a stage-four pancreatic cancer diagnosis in December, with tumors metastasized to his lungs, liver, and vascular and lymphatic systems; the cancer was ruled inoperable and terminal, with doctors estimating three to four months to live.
insights.speaker: Zach Marcus
insights.so_what: Anchors the essay's subject: a prominent public figure given a hard three-to-four-month terminal prognosis who has outlived it.
insights.quote: Last December he announced a diagnosis of stage four pancreatic cancer, which meant tumors had metastasized to his lungs, his liver and his vascular and lymphatic systems.
insights.locator: I'm waiting for Ben to die

insights.claim: Ben Sasse's cancer pain has declined by roughly 80 percent since he began radiation and experimental therapies, because the shrinking tumors no longer press against his spinal column, and he has survived well past his original three-to-four-month prognosis.
insights.speaker: Zach Marcus
insights.so_what: Shows the terminal timeline is fluid; the 'public death' extends indefinitely, reshaping the emotional experience for both subject and audience.
insights.quote: His pain has declined by 80 percent since he began treatment because the tumors have shrunk and no longer press against his spinal column, a victory well worth the constant waves of nausea.
insights.locator: Things are going better than anyone expected

insights.claim: Rather than withdrawing to his family or traveling, Ben Sasse is spending his final days publicly 'modeling how to die,' framing his terminal illness as a deliberate teaching act rather than a private matter.
insights.speaker: Zach Marcus
insights.so_what: Frames public death as a chosen, purposeful performance — a countercultural stance in an era of private, medicalized dying.
insights.quote: Instead of hunkering down with his family, instead of traveling the world, Ben is “redeeming the time” he has left by modeling how to die.
insights.locator: Dying online is a horrific fate

insights.claim: The author reaches Ben Sasse's dying entirely through screens, having formed the attachment via a podcast interview between Sasse and Ross Douthat that surfaced in his YouTube feed, despite never having met or spoken to him.
insights.speaker: Zach Marcus
insights.so_what: Illustrates how a stranger's mortality is now consumed as podcast/video content, mediating intimacy entirely through platforms.
insights.quote: Before his podcast interview with Ross Douthat popped onto my YouTube feed, I knew about Ben Sasse’s life only in its fuzziest outline
insights.locator: You see, I'm not actually friends with Ben

insights.claim: Forming a parasocial attachment to a stranger dying on the internet is described as a common generational experience, with dying now consumed as recurring online content rather than a private event.
insights.speaker: Zach Marcus
insights.so_what: Names a cultural shift: mortality as a mass-mediated, parasocial spectacle native to younger internet audiences.
insights.quote: forming a parasocial attachment to a stranger dying on the internet is quite a common experience for people my age.
insights.locator: You see, I'm not actually friends with Ben

insights.claim: Involuntary online deaths span from instant recorded killings (an ISIS beheading video, watching a bullet rip through Charlie Kirk's neck) to slow, sadistic spectacles like 'lolcows' — internet misfits whose audiences goad their self-destructive behavior toward eventual death.
insights.speaker: Zach Marcus
insights.so_what: Distinguishes coerced/exploitative online death from Sasse's chosen public death — the essay's core contrast about agency and dignity.
insights.quote: The whole genre of internet celebrities known as “lolcows”—online misfits who exist to be bullied and laughed at, whose audiences gleefully goad on the cows’ increasingly depraved and self-destructive behavior.
insights.locator: Other online killings are a slower

insights.claim: The author frames dying online as a horrific fate in which a person is reduced to a meme or video clip 'for eternity,' trapped inside the internet's archive.
insights.speaker: Zach Marcus
insights.so_what: Captures a distinctly digital anxiety: permanent posthumous circulation as content, versus a bounded, dignified death.
insights.quote: Dying online is a horrific fate: trapped inside the bowels of the internet, condemned to slosh around as a meme or a video clip for eternity.
insights.locator: Dying online is a horrific fate

insights.claim: The author reports his own transition from a 'New Atheist determinist' to someone metaphysically inclined to believe in souls, catalyzed by a first-year college seminar called 'The Journey Within.'
insights.speaker: Zach Marcus
insights.so_what: Signals a broader generational drift from confident secular materialism back toward metaphysical or religious openness.
insights.quote: a class partly responsible for my transition from a New Atheist determinist to someone more metaphysically inclined toward believing in things like souls.
insights.locator: For my first-year seminar at college

insights.claim: Marcus observes a 'complete lack of death anxiety' as a through line across classical and religious thinkers — Socrates, Jesus, the Buddha, and Tolstoy's Ivan Ilyich — into which Sasse's own equanimity ('to live is Christ; to die is gain') fits.
insights.speaker: Zach Marcus
insights.so_what: Positions faith-based fearlessness toward death as a counter-model to modern secular dread and the exploitative online death economy.
insights.quote: One through line from that class was the complete lack of death anxiety amongst the thinkers we read.
insights.locator: For my first-year seminar at college
